question: The binary sub-result matches on task (MCI vs CN) but the channel does not: P-117 (correct PDF S1746809423008959, Aljalal et al.) uses resting-state EEG; P-60 (Yamada et al., Computer Speech & Language 81 (2023) 101514) uses tablet-recorded speech features. Condition 1 fails on channel.
metric: Same metric type (accuracy): P-117 binary aMCI vs HC; P-60 binary MCI vs CN sub-result (its headline is the three-class 78.6%).

figures.P-117: 99.81% accuracy (ensemble KNN, 11 NSGA-II channels), binary aMCI vs HC, 10-fold CV over 3660 segment feature vectors from 61 participants; no interval. Wilson 95% with n = 61: z^2/n = 0.06297; centre = (0.9981 + 0.03149)/1.06297 = 0.9686; half-width 0.0314; interval [0.937, 1.000].
figures.P-60: 87.6% MCI vs CN accuracy, nested leave-one-out CV, 89 participants in the binary contrast (46 MCI/43 CN of 114). No interval reported. Wilson with n = 89: z^2/n = 3.8415/89 = 0.04316; centre = (0.876 + 0.02158)/1.04316 = 0.8604; half-width = 1.96*sqrt(0.876*0.124/89 + 3.8415/(4*89^2))/1.04316 = 0.0688; interval [0.792, 0.929].

matched_figure_check: No matched figure exists. Neither paper reports a result in the other's channel; P-117 prints only segment-level accuracies, P-60 participant-level ones. Nothing reconciles the pair.
performance_validity: P-117 meets the Section 3.5 exclusion on its own PDF: 99.81% (>= 0.97), internal 10-fold CV over randomly split segment feature vectors, 61 participants, no external cohort (the round-20 reading's 'likely applies' is confirmed from the correct PDF). P-60's 87.6% is not excluded.
reason: The gap is numerically beyond uncertainty (0.9981 lies outside P-60's Wilson [0.792, 0.929]; 0.876 lies outside P-117's [0.937, 1.000]), but EEG and speech are different measurement channels, so the pair does not address the same clinical question under condition 1. P-117's 99.81% also fails the performance-validity exclusion (condition 5). The record quotes P-60's binary figure correctly.

quotes.quote: With an ensemble KNN classifier, the highest accuracy, 99.81%, is achieved using 11 channels selected by an NSGA-based method.
The combined dataset has 61 people over the age of 55, including 29 amnestic MCI patients and 32 normal cases.

For evaluating the performance of each classifier, we employ 10-fold CV. This method randomly splits the dataset into ten equal subsets, with one subset used for validation (test) and the other nine for training

a machine-learning speech classifier using these features achieved 78.6% accuracy for classifying AD, MCI, and CN through nested cross-validation (AD versus CN: 91.2% accuracy; MCI versus CN: 87.6% accuracy).
Finally, a total of 114 older individuals met the inclusion criteria: 43 CN participants, 46 MCI patients, and 25 AD patients.
We used nested cross-validation with a nested leave-one-out procedure to train classifiers and test their performance.
